fixes.find: where the buoys used to stand.
fixes.replace: where the river markers used to stand.
fixes.why: Buoys don't “stand” in English; this reads like a literal transfer from бакены.

fixes.find: On TV scientists spread their hands over the backwater: all the water has gone, and this stays.
fixes.replace: On TV scientists throw up their hands at the backwater: all the water is gone, but this one is still there.
fixes.why: “Spread their hands” is a Russian gesture calque; “this stays” is also too literal.

fixes.find: I see it from Tanya's window every morning, and every morning I put my palm to the glass, like to a stove.
fixes.replace: I see it from Tanya's window every morning, and every morning I put my palm to the glass as if it were a stove.
fixes.why: “Like to a stove” is not idiomatic English.

fixes.find: since the Tom went
fixes.replace: since the Tom ran dry
fixes.why: The point is that the river dried up; “went” is too vague and calqued.

fixes.find: seventy-two was never
fixes.replace: seventy-two was never going to happen
fixes.why: “Это же никогда” needs an idiomatic English equivalent.

fixes.find: and all these years she's charged it once a month, she doesn't know why herself.
fixes.replace: and all these years she's charged it once a month without knowing why.
fixes.why: The tail phrase is a Russian word order/calque.

fixes.find: I charge it once a month, I don't know why myself.
fixes.replace: I charge it once a month. I don't know why.
fixes.why: “I don't know why myself” is a literal Russian construction.

fixes.find: About myself tomorrow I knew nothing.
fixes.replace: What would happen to me tomorrow, I didn't know.
fixes.why: The current sentence is unidiomatic and too literal.

fixes.find: I lock the door with one turn.
fixes.replace: I turn the lock once.
fixes.why: “На один оборот” has been carried over too mechanically.

fixes.find: I go down to the riverbed by the old fishermen's stairs; the steps lead nowhere now, onto white stones, and I walk over the stones like over sleepers, counting.
fixes.replace: I go down to the riverbed by the old fishermen's stairs; the steps lead nowhere now, onto white stones, and I walk over them as if they were railroad ties, counting.
fixes.why: “Like over sleepers” is unidiomatic, and “sleepers” is British for this American-spelled adaptation.

fixes.find: Sonka answers on the third ring, though in Moscow it's past eleven at night and here it's four in the morning.
fixes.replace: Sonka answers on the third ring, though it's past eleven at night in Moscow and after three in the morning here.
fixes.why: «Четвёртый час утра» is after three, not necessarily four o'clock.

fixes.find: Go on already, you poor thing.
fixes.replace: Go on already, you little disaster.
fixes.why: «Горе луковое» is affectionate scolding, not pity.
fixes.replace_final: Go on already, you silly thing.

fixes.find: I see the drum whole, in the light of my lamp, wet, black, turning evenly and not fast.
fixes.replace: In the beam of my lamp I can see the whole drum, wet and black, turning steadily, not fast.
fixes.why: “I see the drum whole” and “turning evenly” are literal and stiff.

fixes.find: My lamp hits the roof, and the roof spins.
fixes.replace: The beam from my lamp hits the roof, and the roof spins.
fixes.why: The Russian means the lamp light strikes the mine roof; the English sounds like the physical lamp hits it.

fixes.find: At the twentieth step
fixes.replace: On the twentieth step
fixes.why: English counts steps with “on,” not “at,” in this context.

fixes.find: My pant leg flares up, my boot runs.
fixes.replace: My pant leg flares up, and the rubber of my boot starts to run.
fixes.why: Molten rubber can run; “my boot runs” sounds comic/wrong.

fixes.find: The heat comes into my mouth, and I stop breathing before I understand I'm burning.
fixes.replace: Heat fills my mouth, and I stop breathing before I understand I'm burning.
fixes.why: “Comes into my mouth” is too literal and weak for the physical moment.

fixes.find: The last thing I hear is Vitka shouting "Yegor!" down below.
fixes.replace: Down below, Vitka is shouting "Yegor!"
fixes.why: “The last thing I hear” is a stock death-frame; the detail is stronger without it.

fixes.find: "DANGER! BURNING WASTE DUMP"
fixes.replace: "DANGER! BURNING SPOIL HEAP"
fixes.why: This is a burning mining spoil heap, not a garbage dump.

fixes.find: I look at my boot and wait for it to run.
fixes.replace: I look at my boot and wait for the rubber to start running.
fixes.why: Again, the material runs, not the boot itself.

fixes.find: I go fast and right, like in a drill, and I'm glad I didn't run.
fixes.replace: I move fast and do it right, like in a drill, and I'm glad I didn't run.
fixes.why: “Go fast and right” is a Russian construction, not natural English.

fixes.find: It lays the smoke from the upper cracks right on this slope, on me, and at first I hardly see it, just the smell, rotten, sweetish.
fixes.replace: It drives the smoke from the upper cracks straight onto this slope, onto me, and at first I hardly see it, just the smell, rotten, sweetish.
fixes.why: Wind “laying” smoke is too literal here; “drives” keeps the action clear.

fixes.find: Ten meters from Yegorka my knees give.
fixes.replace: Ten meters from Yegorka my knees give way.
fixes.why: The idiom is “knees give way.”

fixes.find: "DANGER! BURNING WASTE DUMP"
fixes.replace: "DANGER! BURNING SPOIL HEAP"
fixes.why: This is a coal spoil heap, not a trash dump.

fixes.find: My throat is raw, like after a pack of Primas on an empty stomach.
fixes.replace: My throat is raw, like after a pack of Prima cigarettes on an empty stomach.
fixes.why: Without the noun, the brand realia is needlessly opaque to an English reader.

fixes.find: I tapped the crust right. I tapped the crust right, and it was the wind that killed me. It blew off the river and laid all the smoke on the slope I was climbing. I should have gone into the wind, from the river side, where the smoke is carried off the slope.
fixes.replace: I tested the crust properly. I tested the crust properly, but the wind killed me. It blew off the river and drove all the smoke onto the slope I was climbing. I should have gone up against the wind, from the river side, where the smoke is carried away from the slope.
fixes.why: Several phrases here are literal Russian: “tapped right,” “it was the wind that,” “laid smoke,” “gone into the wind.”
fixes.replace_final: I tested the crust properly, but the wind killed me. It blew off the river and drove all the smoke onto the slope I was climbing. I should have gone up against the wind, from the river side, where the smoke is carried away from the slope.

verdict: В целом партия крепкая: рабочий голос взрослого Андрея держится, сцены смертей плотные и ясные. Чаще всего мешают русские кальки жестов и синтаксиса, неточные горняцкие/речные реалии вроде dump/buoys, а также несколько стандартных death-scene формул, которые лучше заменить конкретной деталью.
